prayer.text: O Sacrament most holy, O Sacrament divine, all praise and all thanksgiving be every moment thine.

cues.text: A Theft on Horseback
In 1411, in the village of Weiten in Lower Austria, a man stole a consecrated Host and concealed it in his glove before mounting his horse to make for the nearby village of Spitz.
Rather than take the main road, he chose a side route through the valley of Muhldorf.
A Horse That Would Not Move
At a certain point along that side road, the thief's horse abruptly stopped and refused to go any further.
The spot was later marked by a chapel built in memory of the event, no matter how hard he struck it.
Laborers working in the surrounding fields came to help, but between them they could not get the animal to take another step; it stood motionless as though carved from stone.
A Host Dropped Unnoticed
Then, just as suddenly as it had frozen, the horse bolted into a gallop — and in the sudden motion, the Host hidden in the thief's glove fell to the ground without his noticing.
It lay there, unseen, for several days.
Found by a Passerby
A woman named Mrs. Scheck, from the nearby village of Mannersdorf, was passing the spot when she noticed a strong light surrounding something on the ground.
Approaching in wonder, she found the consecrated Host itself, broken into two pieces.
They nonetheless remained joined by fine threads of what appeared to be bleeding flesh.
She recovered it with reverence, and word of the discovery spread quickly through the surrounding villages.
Legacy
Like many medieval Eucharistic traditions built around theft, the Weiten-Raxendorf account centers less on punishing the thief.
The surviving sources do not record his ultimate fate.

Instead, it emphasizes the Host's resistance to being carried away for ordinary or profane purposes, first through the horse's strange behavior and then through the light that led an ordinary passerby to its recovery.
The chapel later built at the site where the horse halted still marks the spot today, a modest rural monument to an episode that has been retold in the surrounding villages for over six centuries.
